sections.learningObjectives:
- Document the completion of an ECG accurately and objectively in the patient's medical record.
- Recognize urgent symptoms, including chest pain and syncope, as potential warning signs.
- Escalate urgent symptoms immediately to licensed staff and follow the facility's emergency procedures.
- Refrain from interpreting ECGs or diagnosing, and instead route all findings to the provider.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

When you finish your homework, you write your name and the date at the top so the teacher knows when you did it. Documenting an ECG is the same: you write down when the test was done so everyone on the care team knows.

### Question 2

Imagine a class where your teacher keeps one big binder of everyone's work. If you put your test in the binder, everyone who needs to see it can find it. The medical record is that binder for the patient.

### Question 3

When you label your lunchbox with your name, the teacher knows it is yours. Labeling an ECG with the patient's name and birth date makes sure the heart tracing goes in the right person's chart.

### Question 4

When you take a picture for a school project, you put it in your folder so the teacher can grade it. The ECG tracing is like that picture: it must go into the chart so the provider can look at it.

### Question 5

Only the person with the special training gets to explain what a complicated picture means. For a heart tracing, that special person is the provider, not the assistant.

### Question 6

If a friend asks what a secret code means and you are not the code expert, you say 'the expert will tell you.' The provider is the expert who explains heart tracings.

### Question 7

A good note tells the facts, like 'the picture was taken at 9 o'clock.' It does not guess what the picture means. Facts only!

### Question 8

If a photo comes out blurry, you do not pretend it is a great photo. You tell someone and take another one. Same idea with a blurry heart tracing.

### Question 9

If you want to see how a plant grows, you take a photo every day and compare them. Heart tracings are compared the same way, so writing the time helps doctors compare them.

### Question 10

When you sign your name on your art project, everyone knows who made it. Signing who did the ECG does the same for the medical record.

### Question 11

A good note says 'the test was done at 9:15 and put in the chart.' It does not try to say what the test means, because only the provider gets to decide that.

### Question 12

If you write the wrong answer in a notebook, you draw one neat line through it and write the right answer next to it, so the teacher can still see the first try. That keeps everything honest.

### Question 13

Before handing out a test, a teacher checks the student's name twice to give it to the right person. Checking a patient's name and birth date does the same.

### Question 14

If you turn in a test but the teacher has not graded it yet, you still write down that you turned it in. The note says 'done, waiting for the provider to review.'

### Question 15

The assistant can write down what happened, like 'test done at 9:15.' Deciding what the test means is the provider's job, not the assistant's.

### Question 16

To see if a cut is healing, you take a photo today and one tomorrow and compare them side by side. Writing the time on each ECG lets doctors compare them the same way.

### Question 17

If a friend says 'my chest feels squished,' you would not just keep playing. You would tell a grown-up right away. The assistant does the same by telling the provider.

### Question 18

A good journal entry tells the truth, just the facts, and is written the same day. Medical notes follow the same three rules.

### Question 19

If the printer breaks while doing a project, you tell the teacher and try again. You do not pretend the project printed. The assistant does the same with a broken ECG machine.

### Question 20

Some things are private, like a diary. A patient's heart test is private too, so it stays locked away and is shared only with the people caring for them.

### Question 21

If the teacher says 'make sure your test is turned in,' you put it in the right folder right away. The assistant puts the ECG note and tracing in the chart right away.

### Question 22

When everyone on a team writes down what they did, the next person knows exactly what happened. That is how the care team stays on the same page.

### Question 23

The assistant writes down 'the test happened.' Figuring out what the test shows is the provider's job. Two different jobs!

### Question 24

If you finish a chore but the adult in charge is out, you leave a note saying 'done, please check.' That note is exactly what the assistant leaves in the chart.

### Question 25

A worksheet with labeled boxes helps you not forget any answers. The ECG template is a labeled worksheet for the chart.

### Question 26

Saying 'looks normal' is like a student grading their own test before the teacher does. The assistant should just say 'test done' and let the provider grade it.

### Question 27

Before writing in a notebook, you check it is the right notebook and write the date. The assistant checks the right chart and writes the date and time first.

### Question 28

If you do not know which box to write in, you ask the teacher instead of guessing. The assistant asks the supervisor instead of guessing.

### Question 29

If you finish a late homework assignment, you tell the teacher 'this is late' and write today's date. You do not pretend it was on time.

### Question 30

A complete recipe lists all the ingredients and steps. A complete ECG note lists the patient, the time, who did it, and what happened to the tracing.

### Question 31

The heart's biggest 'help me' signal is a feeling of squeezing or pain in the chest. It is like a fire alarm for the heart.

### Question 32

The pain can travel like a phone signal moving from one tower to another, going from the chest to the arm, back, neck, jaw, or belly.

### Question 33

A heart problem can show up in more ways than chest pain, like feeling short of breath, sweaty, sick to the stomach, or dizzy.

### Question 34

Syncope is the doctor's word for fainting, when someone suddenly 'blacks out' for a short time.

### Question 35

Three warning bells at once, chest tightness plus trouble breathing plus sweating, mean you ring the alarm right away, not later.

### Question 36

Not every heart attack announces itself the same way, like not every birthday party has the same kind of cake. Some are obvious, some are quiet.

### Question 37

If a fire alarm rings and then stops, you still tell a grown-up, because the danger might not be gone. A chest pain that went away still needs to be reported.

### Question 38

Pain that starts in the chest and travels to the arm and jaw is a well-known heart warning sign, like a storm warning flag.

### Question 39

If someone says 'I feel like I might fall over,' you help them sit safely and call for help. You do not walk away.

### Question 40

Nearly fainting is like a wobble before a fall. You steady the person and get help before they actually fall.

### Question 41

Chest discomfort plus feeling sick and clammy is like several warning lights turning on at once in a car. You stop and get help.

### Question 42

The assistant is not the person who can tell a harmless tummy ache from a heart problem, so they hand it to the provider, like calling a grown-up when unsure.

### Question 43

Some people's hearts send quieter signals, especially if they have diabetes. So even a small 'I feel off' should be taken seriously.

### Question 44

Someone pale, sweaty, and grabbing their chest needs help right now, and someone should stay with them the whole time.

### Question 45

Suddenly being unable to catch your breath while sitting still is a warning sign, like a smoke alarm going off for no clear reason.

### Question 46

Fainting is serious on its own, and hitting your head makes it even more serious, so help is needed right away.

### Question 47

Passing out is the body's way of saying something might be very wrong, so it is always treated as important.

### Question 48

Some signs are quiet, but chest pressure with trouble breathing and sweating is a loud 'get help now' signal.

### Question 49

When someone says 'I'm about to pass out,' you help them sit or lie down safely and call for help, not walk away.

### Question 50

The experts list many warning signs: chest pain, trouble breathing, and pain in the jaw, neck, back, arm, or shoulder.

### Question 51

Sometimes a grown-up's 'something is off' feeling is right. When a patient looks wrong, you ask for help instead of shrugging it off.

### Question 52

A warning light that flickers on and off still means something is wrong. Chest pain that comes and goes still needs to be reported.

### Question 53

Deciding what chest pain means is the provider's special job. The assistant's job is to recognize it and call for the provider.

### Question 54

Breaking out in a cold sweat while the chest hurts is a well-known heart warning sign, like the body's own red flag.

### Question 55

Sometimes a heart problem shows up as pain in the jaw or neck instead of the chest. That is why these odd symptoms still get reported.

### Question 56

The assistant is the look-out who spots the warning sign and calls the expert, not the one who decides what the sign means.

### Question 57

A heart problem can sometimes pretend to be a stomach ache, with nausea and sweating. That is why these symptoms get checked by the provider.

### Question 58

A heart problem can show up as trouble breathing and feeling dizzy, even when the chest does not hurt. So those signs still trigger the alarm.

### Question 59

When you are not sure if something is dangerous, it is safer to call for help. Better safe than sorry.

### Question 60

Sometimes people say 'it is nothing' because they do not want to worry anyone. The safe choice is still to get it checked right away.

### Question 61

The first thing you do when you hear a fire alarm is tell a grown-up. The assistant tells the provider right away when a patient has chest pain.

### Question 62

If no grown-up is nearby and someone is in trouble, you call 911. The assistant follows the office's emergency plan, which can mean calling 911.

### Question 63

You never leave a hurt friend alone; you stay with them and get help. The assistant stays with the patient and gets help.

### Question 64

The assistant is not the one who reads the heart tracing; the provider is. So the assistant points the patient to the provider for answers.

### Question 65

If someone is fainting, you gently help them to the ground so they do not fall and get hurt, then you call for help.

### Question 66

When someone wakes up after fainting, you keep them lying down, make sure they are safe, and get help. You wait before giving them anything to drink.

### Question 67

Only the expert gets to decide about medicine for chest pain. The assistant's job is to get the expert, not to hand out pills.

### Question 68

A fire drill plan tells everyone exactly what to do so no one panics. The office emergency plan does the same for a heart attack.

### Question 69

Knowing where the first-aid kit is and how to call 911 means you can help fast when someone needs it.

### Question 70

When you are not sure if something is safe, you ask for help instead of guessing. Same rule at the doctor's office.

### Question 71

The assistant writes down facts, like what the patient said and when the test was done. Saying 'this is a heart attack' is the provider's job.

### Question 72

Reading a heart tracing is a special skill, like reading sheet music. The trained expert, the clinician, is the one who does it.

### Question 73

When someone asks about a test result, the assistant says 'the provider will explain it,' just like saying 'ask the teacher.'

### Question 74

After telling a grown-up about a problem, you also write down what happened so it is not forgotten. The assistant writes down the report and the actions taken.

### Question 75

You get help without leaving the person who needs it, by calling out or pressing the call button while staying right there.

### Question 76

Getting an ambulance fast gives someone the best chance, like getting a fire truck there quickly when there is a fire.

### Question 77

When the ambulance arrives, the assistant stays with the patient, shares what happened, and hands over the chart, like passing the baton in a relay.

### Question 78

When the warning bell rings, you act right away, not after waiting a while. Chest pain gets reported the moment it is known.

### Question 79

The assistant is like a helpful teammate who spots problems, writes things down, and calls the expert, not the one who makes the big medical calls.

### Question 80

If a patient feels chest pressure during the test, you take care of them and tell the provider right away, not keep going quietly.

### Question 81

Even if a test looks simple, only the teacher grades it. The assistant passes every tracing to the provider, no matter how it looks.

### Question 82

After someone faints, you keep an eye on them until help comes, because things can change quickly and they might faint again.

### Question 83

When something is wrong, you tell the person in charge, not just anyone. The assistant reports to the provider, nurse, or supervisor.

### Question 84

Even if the pain stopped, the patient should be checked before leaving, like making sure the stove is off before leaving the house.

### Question 85

You write down who you told and when, so later everyone knows what happened. The assistant writes the same about the chest-pain report.

### Question 86

Someone may say 'it is just heartburn,' but the assistant still gets the provider to check, because chest discomfort is always taken seriously.

### Question 87

If a grown-up is busy, you still interrupt for an emergency. A patient fainting is the kind of emergency that interrupts.

### Question 88

Deciding what a heart tracing means is a job for someone with special training, like only a lifeguard decides who needs rescue.

### Question 89

Even if someone asks nicely, the assistant does not read the heart tracing, because that is the provider's special job.

### Question 90

The assistant's three jobs are: write down the test was done, notice warning signs, and get help fast. Not read the test or decide what it means.
